title: Chromatography
aim: To use paper chromatography to separate the coloured substances in food colourings, identify them by comparison with known dyes, and calculate their Rf values.
background: Paper chromatography separates the substances in a mixture. It has two phases: the stationary phase is the paper, and the mobile phase is the solvent (for example water) that moves up the paper.

Each substance is distributed between the two phases. A substance that is more soluble in the solvent and less attracted to the paper spends more time in the mobile phase, so it moves further up the paper. Different substances move different distances, so they separate into different spots.

The Rf value of a substance is the distance moved by the substance divided by the distance moved by the solvent: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent. Rf values are always between 0 and 1. In the same solvent and conditions, a substance always has the same Rf value, so Rf values can be used to identify substances.
A pure substance produces a single spot in every solvent. A mixture (formulation) usually produces two or more spots. A substance that does not dissolve in the solvent stays on the start line.
hypothesis: The food colourings that are mixtures will separate into more than one spot, and spots with the same Rf values as known dyes will be the same substances as those dyes.

variables.independent: The sample of food colouring or dye spotted on the paper.
variables.dependent: The distance moved by each spot, used to calculate its Rf value; the number of spots.
control: Solvent (water) and its depth in the beaker (below the start line)
Height of the start line (1.5 cm from the bottom)
Temperature and time allowed for the solvent to move
Lid on the beaker so the air inside stays saturated with solvent vapour

equipment: 250 cm³ beaker (or chromatography tank) with a lid or watch glass
Capillary tubes or fine glass rods for spotting
Samples of known dyes (A, B, C, D) and unknown food colourings (X and Y)
Glass rod or wooden splint and paper clip to hang the paper
method: Use a pencil and ruler to draw a straight start line (baseline) 1.5 cm above the bottom edge of the chromatography paper.
Mark small pencil dots along the line, at least 1.5 cm apart, one for each sample. Label each dot in pencil underneath (A, B, C, D, X, Y).
Use a capillary tube to put a small spot of each sample on its dot. Let it dry, then add another spot on top to make it more concentrated. Keep the spots small.
Pour water into the beaker to a depth of about 1 cm, so that the water level will be below the start line.

Hang the paper from a glass rod (using a paper clip) so that the bottom edge dips into the water but the start line and spots stay above the water level. The paper must not touch the sides of the beaker.
Put a lid on the beaker and leave it undisturbed while the water soaks up the paper.
When the solvent is about 1 cm from the top of the paper, remove the paper and immediately mark the position of the solvent front with a pencil line.
Measure the distance from the start line to the solvent front.
For each spot, measure the distance from the start line to the centre of the spot.
Calculate the Rf value of each spot using Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent.
Compare the number of spots and the Rf values of the unknown food colourings with those of the known dyes.

safety.risk: May stain skin and clothing, and some dyes are irritants.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection, handle the paper by its edges and wash hands after the practical.

safety.hazard: Organic solvents such as ethanol (if used instead of water)
safety.risk: Highly flammable; vapour can be harmful if breathed in.
safety.precaution: Keep away from naked flames, keep a lid on the container and use a well-ventilated room.
Handle gently and put broken glass in the broken glass bin.

results.notes: Distance moved by solvent (start line to solvent front) = 8.0 cm. Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ 8.0 cm. For example, dye A: 2.4 ÷ 8.0 = 0.30. Rf values have no units. Measure to the centre of each spot.

analysis: Dyes A, B, C and D each gave a single spot, which suggests that each is a pure substance (in this solvent).
Food colouring X separated into two spots, so it is a mixture. Its spots had Rf values of 0.30 and 0.70, which match dye A and dye B, so X contains dyes A and B.

Food colouring Y also gave two spots, so it is a mixture. One spot (Rf 0.50) matches dye C. The other stayed on the start line (Rf 0), so this substance is insoluble in water; it cannot be identified using this solvent and would need a different solvent.
Dye D (Rf 0.80) moved furthest, so it is the most soluble in water and/or the least attracted to the paper. Dye A (Rf 0.30) is less soluble in the solvent and/or more strongly attracted to the paper.
Rf values only match if the same solvent and paper are used, so the known dyes must be run on the same chromatogram as the unknown samples.

errors.error: Spots that are too large spread out and overlap, making the distances hard to measure.
errors.improvement: Use a fine capillary tube to make small spots, and build up concentration by spotting several times, letting each dry in between.

errors.error: The solvent front evaporates and becomes hard to see if not marked straight away.
errors.improvement: Mark the solvent front with pencil as soon as the paper is removed, and keep a lid on the beaker during the run.

errors.error: Measuring to the top or bottom of a spot instead of its centre gives inaccurate Rf values.
errors.improvement: Always measure from the start line to the centre of each spot.

errors.error: If the solvent level is above the start line, the samples dissolve into the solvent in the beaker instead of moving up the paper.
errors.improvement: Make sure the solvent depth is less than the height of the start line (for example 1 cm of water, start line at 1.5 cm).

examTips: Learn the Rf equation: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent. Rf has no units and is always less than 1.
Draw the start line in pencil, not ink: pencil (graphite) is insoluble so it does not move, but ink would dissolve and run up the paper.
The solvent level must be below the start line, otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.
One spot means a pure substance; more than one spot means a mixture. To identify a substance, match both the colour and the Rf value with a known substance.
Name the phases: the paper is the stationary phase and the solvent is the mobile phase. Separation happens because substances are distributed differently between the two phases.

questions.question: Why is the start line drawn in pencil and not in ink?
options: Pencil is easier to see when the paper is wet
Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent, but ink would and would move up the paper
Ink would react with the solvent
Pencil helps the solvent move up the paper
markScheme: 1 mark: pencil (graphite) is insoluble / does not move with the solvent, whereas ink would dissolve and separate
questions.explanation: Ink is itself a mixture of dyes. It would dissolve in the solvent and produce extra spots, confusing the results.

questions.question:
On a chromatogram, the solvent moved 8.0 cm from the start line. A spot moved 3.2 cm from the start line.
Calculate the Rf value of the spot.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.40
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent = 3.2 ÷ 8.0 = 0.40. Dividing the other way gives 2.5, which is impossible because Rf must be less than 1.

questions.question: In paper chromatography, what is the stationary phase?
options: The solvent
The sample spot
The lid of the beaker
The paper
markScheme: 1 mark: the paper
questions.explanation: The stationary phase does not move: in paper chromatography it is the paper. The solvent is the mobile phase.

questions.question: Explain why the solvent level must be below the start line.
acceptedAnswers: spots would dissolve into the solvent
samples wash off into the solvent
samples would not move up the paper
markScheme: 1 mark: otherwise the spots / samples would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker (instead of moving up the paper)
questions.explanation: The samples need to be carried up the paper by the solvent. If they sit under the solvent surface, they just dissolve into the bulk liquid.

questions.question: A food colouring produces three spots on a chromatogram. What does this show?
options: It is a pure substance
It contains at least three different substances
It is insoluble in the solvent
The solvent was too deep
markScheme: 1 mark: it is a mixture of at least three substances
questions.explanation: Each spot is a different substance. It is 'at least' three because two substances could have the same Rf value in this solvent and appear as one spot.

questions.question:
Food colouring X gave spots with Rf values of 0.30 and 0.70. Dye A has an Rf value of 0.30, dye B has 0.70 and dye C has 0.50.
What can you conclude about food colouring X? Explain your answer.
acceptedAnswers: same Rf values as A and B
markScheme: 1 mark: X is a mixture that contains dyes A and B (not C)
1 mark: because its spots have the same Rf values (and colours) as A and B
questions.explanation: Matching Rf values in the same solvent show the substances are probably the same. X has no spot at Rf 0.50, so it does not contain dye C.

questions.question: One substance in food colouring Y stayed on the start line. Explain why, and suggest how the student could find out what it is.
acceptedAnswers: does not dissolve in the solvent
markScheme: 1 mark: the substance is insoluble in the solvent (water)
1 mark: repeat the chromatography using a different solvent (for example ethanol) and compare with known substances
questions.explanation: A substance can only move up the paper if it dissolves in the mobile phase. A different solvent may dissolve it and let it be identified.

questions.question: Why is a lid placed on the beaker during chromatography?
options: To stop the solvent evaporating from the paper, so the solvent front moves steadily
To keep light out so the dyes do not fade
To stop the paper falling into the solvent
To make the spots move faster by heating
markScheme: 1 mark: to stop the solvent evaporating (keep the air saturated with solvent vapour)
questions.explanation: If solvent evaporated from the paper, the solvent front would move unevenly and the Rf values would be unreliable. A lid also reduces the release of flammable or harmful solvent vapour.

questions.question:
A spot has an Rf value of 0.65. The solvent moved 9.0 cm from the start line.
Calculate how far the spot moved from the start line.
markScheme: 1 mark: distance = Rf × distance moved by solvent = 0.65 × 9.0
1 mark: 5.85 cm (accept 5.9 cm)
questions.explanation: Rearrange Rf = substance distance ÷ solvent distance to give substance distance = Rf × solvent distance = 0.65 × 9.0 = 5.85 cm.

questions.question: Give two reasons why it is important to keep the sample spots small.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: large spots spread and overlap with other spots; small spots separate more clearly; it is easier to find the centre of a small spot, giving more accurate Rf values
questions.explanation: Large spots produce long smears. Their centres are hard to locate, and neighbouring substances may not separate.

questions.question: Dye D has a higher Rf value than dye A in water. Which statement explains this?
options: Dye D is more strongly attracted to the paper than dye A
Dye D is less soluble in water than dye A
Dye D spends more time in the mobile phase than dye A
Dye D has a larger spot than dye A
markScheme: 1 mark: dye D spends more time in the mobile phase (more soluble in the solvent / less attracted to the paper)
questions.explanation: Substances that are more soluble in the solvent, or less attracted to the stationary phase, move further. Spot size does not change the Rf value.

questions.question: A student says that because a dye gave one spot in water, it must be a pure substance. Evaluate this statement.
acceptedAnswers: two substances could have the same Rf value
markScheme: 1 mark: it suggests the dye is pure, but two substances could have the same Rf value in water (or one could be insoluble and hidden on the start line)
1 mark: it should be tested in other solvents; a pure substance gives a single spot in all solvents
questions.explanation: One spot in one solvent is good evidence but not proof. Running the dye in a second solvent, or checking its melting point, would confirm it is pure.

questions.question: Which of these could be an Rf value?
options: 6.2 cm
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.62
questions.explanation: Rf values are between 0 and 1 because a substance cannot move further than the solvent. Rf values have no units.

questions.question:
A spot moved 34 mm from the start line. The solvent front was 8.5 cm from the start line.
Calculate the Rf value of the spot.
markScheme: 1 mark: converts to the same units: 34 mm = 3.4 cm (or 8.5 cm = 85 mm)
questions.explanation: Both distances must be in the same units before dividing. 34 ÷ 8.5 = 4.0 is wrong because it mixes millimetres and centimetres.

questions.question:
Describe how to use paper chromatography to find out whether a food colouring contains any of three known dyes, A, B and C.
Include how you would use Rf values.
markScheme: Indicative content: draw a pencil start line about 1.5 cm from the bottom of the paper; put small spots of the food colouring and dyes A, B and C on the line, spaced apart; add solvent (water) to a beaker to a depth below the start line; hang the paper so the bottom dips into the solvent, not touching the sides; put a lid on; leave until the solvent is near the top; remove and mark the solvent front in pencil; dry; measure distance moved by solvent and by the centre of each spot from the start line; Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent; compare Rf values and colours: spots in the food colouring with the same Rf as a known dye show that dye is present; number of spots shows how many substances are present
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent method with correct setup details (pencil line, solvent below line, lid, solvent front), how to calculate Rf values and how to use them to identify the dyes.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with most setup details and a reference to comparing spots or Rf values.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as put spots on paper in water and see how far they go.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The question asks how Rf values are used. Good answers explain how the measurements are taken and that matching Rf values (in the same solvent) identify substances.
